There's a couple of basic features that I'd really like to see added to the inbox. The first is a way of distinguishing messages in your inbox that have already been read from those that have not -- either highlighting unread messages in a separate color, or doing what reddit does and having a separate tab for unread messages. The way it is now it's really easy to miss replies when you have more than one waiting for you.

The second, related suggestion is a "mark unread" button. Sometimes I'll check a message but not be up to a fleshed out response at the time I read it, and want to save it for later. This is easy on both reddit and basically every e-mail system on the planet, but Voat currently lacks the functionality.

Finally, a reddit style "context" button would be really nice for posts in your inbox and on your profile. Currently we only have a "parent" button, when a button to show the full threaded discussion like reddit's "context" button would be really helpful.

The short list definitely includes Doom, Mario, Commands & Conquer, the usual genre defining games. But those are all genres that are still with us.

But lets take a moment to remember genres of years past.

Kings Quest was enormous influential. Sierra pioneered graphical adventures, along with sound design. I was reading through some old issues of Computer Gaming World from before the age of 3D graphics, and back then they were all about sound cards. And the gold standard for sound cards was how well did a Sierra Adventure game sound. Just wrap your mind around that for a minute. Imagine all the attention to detail that is paid to video benchmarks, and now imagine that applied to the sound in a Sierra adventure game instead.

Lets also take a moment to remember Wizardry, probably the most well known progenitor of the dungeon crawl, party based RPG. I recently rage quit my playthrough of it, as it's not without it's faults. But it set in stone the formula of a party of characters exploring a fixed dungeon you had to map out, full of tricks and traps. It even has a basic job switching system and prestige classes. This is a genre that has all but died, with only Legend of Grimrock in recent memory carrying the torch. But back in the day, it spawned innumerable series. Bard's Tale, Might & Magic, Eye of the Beholder, Lands of Lore, Pool of Radiance and probably more I'm forgetting.

And no list of influential games for dead genres would be complete without Zork. Zork had it's own antecedents. Adventure most notably. But it's my understanding as I read through the history of gaming that Zork made innovations in developing the parser for text adventure games. It's hard to understand just how huge the industry of text adventure games was, both before and after Zork. It's a subject I've actually been reading a lot about lately and find quite fascinating. It's just a shame Zork stumbled, and hard, when it entered the graphical age. First with the hit or miss Beyond Zork, and then with the GRIMDARK Zork Nemesis. Sadly, right as Zork found its Zorkiness again in Zork: Grand Inquisitor, the series was permanently shelved. If only we'd seen the rest of that planned trilogy.
Super Mario 64 arguably codified the standards for 3D platforming games, influencing a large amount of 3D platformers up to now.

I'd add Crash Bandicoot to that as well. Both games knocked it out of the park as the first two big 3D platformers and immediately proved it was a viable type of game.

The funny thing is that they had vastly different designs (specifically the Open Level design of SM64 and the more linear, closed design of Crash) but both nailed their own design so well that they created an entire genre. Having 2 early games that were the same genre but so different helped keep future 3D platformers from being shoehorned into one design or another as well, which enabled the genre to take off better.

If we're naming early 3D platformers that did it right, Tomb Raider deserves a nod too. TR, Crash Bandicoot, and Super Mario 64 all came out within a few months of each other in 1996. Each tried to do a different thing (TR's target audience was completely different from the others) and succeeded in different ways.
Half Life 2 basically invented the realtime cutscene, and was widely considered the explosion of the campaign FPS genre and the true birth of the Valve corporation.
Zelda on the gold cartridge. Deep story, challenging dungeons, ability to save your progress.

Civilization put "god games" on the map. It helped create the market for strategy games and tycoon games and its effects can be attributed to the success of Starcraft, Total War and many other great strategy games that joined the market it helped build.

Grand Theft Auto III inspired games in many genres to take an open world approach. Half-Life was a major change in how level design and narrative worked in shooters. Demon's Souls is a game that is going to seem more and more influential as time passes and seamless co-op and adversarial modes are worked into what would otherwise be completely single player experiences.
Counter-Strike. Really put mods on the map to be taken seriously by developers.

Super Mario Bros, Doom, Super Mario 64, Final Fantasy 7

just a few of the most significant games of all time, when it comes to ushering in huge changes in how games were perceived and designed.
